4. On the question of amendment of the pleadings the opinions the superior Courts of this sub-continent are almost identical. It is that an amendment to the pleadings can be made at any stage of the proceedings but such amendment cannot be made if the nature and character of the suit is changed; that the amendment is barred on the date of institution of the suit; that the amendment should be allowed with a view to resolving all controversies over the same subject matter between the parties and this will prevent the multi-furiousness of proceedings; that all reliefs ancillary to the main relief which is in the nature of additional relief should be allowed as general rule. The averments in the plaint and written statements are pleadings, but in respect of amendment of the written statement the Code is a bit more liberal, inasmuch as, there is also a provision in the Code to file additional written statement under Order 8, Rule 9 of the Code. Secondly, as regards the question of limitation both the plaintiffs and defendants are not standing on the same footing, inasmuch as, the question of limitation does not arise in case of the amendment of the written statement. 

 8. In Indian Jurisdiction similar views have been taken in Leach V. Jardine Skinner, AIR 1957 SC 357. It has been observed in Para 16 that 'Courts would, as a rule, decline to allow amendments, if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation on the date of the application. But that is a factor to be taken into account in exercise of the discretion as to whether amendment should be ordered and does not affect the power of the Court to order it, if that is required in the interest of justice'. In another case of the same issue, in Pirgonda Hongonda Patil V. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, AIR 1957 SC 363, the question was whether the addition of a relief or reliefs in a suit would change the nature and character of the suit. It was observed that it is not feasible nor advisable to encase a discretionary power within the strait jacket on an inflexible formula. In that case there was defect in the plaint that stood in the way of the plaintiff in getting the relief and despite pointing out the defect by the defendant no amendment was made in the trial Court and the suit was dismissed on the ground of such defect. In the High Court the prayer for amendment was allowed at the appellate stage. The respondent objected to the amendment on the ground that the amendment was barred by limitation on the date of the prayer since the appellant by filing petition raised the defect at the trial stage. The Court observed that the quality and quantity of the reliefs sought remain the same; whether the relief should be granted or not is a different matter as to which Court is not called upon to express any opinion at the stage of amendment. The Court then with approval of the views taken by Batchelor, J. in 32 Bomb 644 observed as under: 

 "All amendments ought to be allowed which satisfy the two conditions (a) of not working injustice to the other side, and (b) of being necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties .... But I refrain from citing further authorities, as, in my opinion, they all lay down precisely the same doctrine. That doctrine, as I understand it, is that amendment should be refused only where the other party cannot be placed in the same position as if the pleading had been originally correct, but the amendment would cause him an injury which could not be compensated in costs. It is merely a particular case of this general rule that where a plaintiff seeks to amend by setting up a fresh claim in respect of a cause of action which since the institution of the suit has become barred by limitation, the amendment must be refused; to allow it would be to cause the defendant an injury which could not be compensated in costs by depriving him of a good defence to the claim. The ultimate test therefore still remains the same; can the amendment be allowed without injustice to the other side, or can it not ?"
